summary: Explains that renumbering routers involves more than addresses and routes, since routers interact with servers such as DNS and SNMP. It is an informational guide to the things to consider.

eli5.summary: When you change a router's address, other helpers that know it must also be told.

questions: what breaks when you renumber a router
why use dns names in router configurations
what is a flag day cutover
subtitle: Changing a network's IP addresses touches far more than the routes: names, filters, servers and neighbours all remember the old numbers.

tldr.problem: Organizations often have to change their IP addresses, and routers are the devices most tied to the numbering plan. Router configurations also point at DNS, SNMP, DHCP and other servers by address, so a change ripples outward.
tldr.mechanism: The guide walks through why networks renumber, how to scope the change by prefix, how to make the network easier to renumber first, which router settings hold addresses, and a step-by-step plan for the cutover.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational checklist, not a protocol. It has since been updated by RFC 4192, and it does not claim to be a comparison of products.

today: RFC 2072 is an Informational RFC and has been updated by RFC 4192. It is a planning guide rather than a protocol, so it has no conformance requirements of its own.

sections.title: Why Networks Renumber
sections.content:
RFC 2072 covers the router side of a renumbering effort, once the decision to renumber has been made. The overall motivations are in RFC 2071. The guide is meant to be vendor-independent, and it warns that not every feature it mentions exists on every router.

Reasons to renumber can be technical, organizational or both, and the guide says the organizational reasons should be defined first to justify the budget. Examples it gives: changing Internet Service Providers, because under CIDR an organization's addresses have to change when it moves to a new provider (quoting RFC 1900); moving from bridging to routing; adding workgroup switches or virtual LANs; and adopting frame relay or other nonbroadcast multiaccess (NBMA) services.

Two examples show how technology forces a change. A set of switches forms one broadcast domain, and each broadcast domain should map to a single IP subnet. And on NBMA services it is often better to treat each virtual circuit as its own subnet, which calls for /30 prefixes and so for routers that support variable length subnet masks.

The introduction gives a seven-point plan: state the reason, understand the numbering principles, make the network renumbering-friendly, know the pitfalls, identify tools, evaluate the affected router mechanisms, and set up a transition plan.
sections.eli5: People move house for different reasons: a new job, a bigger family, a new neighbourhood. Networks change addresses for similar reasons, and whatever the reason, it is a big job that needs a plan.

sections.title: Prefixes and the Scope of Renumbering
sections.content:
A router looks at the leftmost bits of a packet's destination address, called a prefix, and looks that prefix up in its routing table (formally the Forwarding Information Base). If there is no match, the router returns an ICMP Destination Unreachable message to the source. The guide stresses that routers decide on the total prefix and do not know or care where the subnet boundary falls.

Renumbering is easier to scope by asking who controls which bits. The high-order part is often assigned by a registry or an ISP (a CIDR block), and the enterprise extends the prefix to the right to make subnets. The change can touch the high-order part, the low-order part, or both. Prefixes from the private address space of RFC 1918 are an enterprise-local decision.

The guide advises taking an inventory in which each prefix is unaffected, old (to be renumbered or retired) or new. Renumbering is easiest when each old prefix maps to one new prefix, but the ideal often cannot be reached and old and new space may have to run in parallel. Impact is expected to be greatest high in a hierarchy of backbone and regional routers, and least in stub parts that have a single route to the backbone.
sections.eli5: An address is like a street address read from left to right: country first, then town, then street. Routers only need the first part to pass a letter along. Changing the first part, the last part or both makes different amounts of work.

sections.title: Making a Network Renumbering-Friendly
sections.content:
Before any prefix changes, the guide suggests reducing the number of places where an address is written down. Wherever possible, replace hard-coded addresses with more flexible mechanisms, and make configuration changes offline on a server and then download them to the router.

Specific advice: use default routes for stub routers and for boundary routers with a single ISP; summarize routes as far as practical, because if every renumbered bit lies to the right of the summarized prefix length the change can be invisible to the rest of the routing system; and refer to servers by DNS name rather than by IP address, documenting any router that only supports explicit addresses.

DNS helps but has its own traps. Routers can cache learned names, so a restart or an explicit cache clear may be needed, and router configurations may hold static name-to-address entries that DNS changes will not touch. During a transition the new address can be added as an extra A record, and PTR reverse entries should exist for new addresses because some vendor tools depend on them.

Dynamic addressing (DHCP, BOOTP, PPP) reduces the places that need edits, and routers may assign addresses or forward requests to a server. Network address translation (NAT) can reduce how much must be renumbered, but the guide says it must not be regarded as a panacea: it interferes with protocols that carry IP addresses as data, such as TCP and UDP checksums, ICMP messages, DNS queries and the FTP PORT command.
sections.eli5: If your address is written on only one list, moving is easy. If it is scribbled on hundreds of sticky notes, it is a mess. So first collect the notes into one place, and use names instead of numbers where you can.

sections.title: Pitfalls With Classless Routing
sections.content:
A big reason to renumber is to get globally routable space, which in the Internet is allocated by arbitrary-length prefix (CIDR). Inside an enterprise the same idea is called variable length subnet masking (VLSM). The guide lists the rules that must be followed: allow the all-zeroes and all-ones subnets (RFC 1812), do not assume a route to a Class A, B or C network number implies routes to all its subnets, and do not infer a prefix length from the first octet. Many routers, and more hosts, do not follow them. It suggests moving a RIPv1 environment to RIPv2, using a default route toward a CIDR-capable provider, or using CIDR-compliant static routes.

The guide's example of discontiguous networks uses a classful (RIPv1) system of three routers. Router 1 and Router 3 each aggregate their 10.x.0.0/16 subnets into 10.0.0.0/8 and advertise it to Router 2 over 172.31.0.0/16 links. Router 2 then has two advertisements of 10.0.0.0 on different interfaces and cannot tell which way a subnet lies, and connectivity between Routers 1 and 3 breaks too. Workarounds include a classless protocol, an IP-over-IP tunnel through Router 2, or secondary addresses with filtering.

Hosts that do not understand prefix lengths can sometimes be shielded with proxy ARP, with a deliberate host misconfiguration that makes them ARP for every destination, or by running passive RIP. The guide also warns about duplicate MAC addresses on router interfaces (for example from DECnet or IPX), and about caches, DHCP, DNS, SNMP and TCP tunnels that still point at old addresses.
sections.eli5: Old routers are like people who only understand whole-street addresses. If you split a street into little pieces they get confused, so you have to either teach them or give them a helper who understands.

sections.title: Router Settings That Hold Addresses
sections.content:
The middle of the guide goes setting by setting. Router identifiers: protocols like OSPF and BGP need an address for the router itself. Letting the router pick its highest address by default can be unstable and is not recommended; the guide prefers an explicitly configured ID, which can come from RFC 1918 private space if it is only a local 32-bit identifier. Interface addresses may need an explicit mask where an old classful default was used. Giving an interface both old and new addresses helps a transition, but OSPF and IS-IS may not advertise the extra ones, and removing the old ones probably needs a restart.

Unnumbered interfaces make management harder, and a move to classless addressing lets serial links use /30 prefixes instead. Address resolution statements for NBMA and switched media (frame relay DLCIs, X.121, SMDS, ATM, telephone numbers) must be changed to the new address. Under RFC 1812 routers must not forward limited broadcasts to 255.255.255.255, so serverless segments often translate them to a directed broadcast or a host address, and that rule must be edited too.

Filters and firewalls carry addresses and prefix lengths, and they hold security policy, so they need extreme care. A length change can be hard to spot when the rule is at a higher level of aggregation. Dynamic rules inserted by RADIUS or TACACS+ and stateful packet screening databases are extensions of router configuration.

Routing: static routes may need a restart or explicit clear. RIPv1 is described as Historic and to be avoided in new plans. OSPF router IDs, summarization and area boundaries are sensitive, and IS-IS area definitions may change with prefixes. BGP is the most complex, since the router ID, peer addresses, prefix lists and filter rules are all hard-coded, other autonomous systems and routing registries refer to them, and route objects must be deleted and added. Network management scripts, TFTP and SNMP servers, trap and syslog destinations and NTP references often hold addresses, and SNMP databases are usually organized by IP address. Tunnels can carry legacy addresses over a renumbered network, and the guide suggests reserving space for future IPv6 tunnels.
sections.eli5: Inside a router there are many little places where an address is written: its own name tag, its neighbours' phone numbers, the guest list at the door. When you change the address, each of those places needs fixing.

sections.title: Tools, Planning and the Cutover
sections.content:
The guide imagines simple tools that search configuration files for affected addresses and names, then rewrite them. Its address modification functions are zerobits(position,length), which clears bits, and orbits(position,length,newbits), which ORs in new ones. It reminds readers that dotted decimal can hide which bits are changing, so work in binary. Naming needs a list of name-to-address mappings, including static ones inside routers, compared with the affected prefixes.

The plan has these steps: inventory the affected addresses and names; design any topology changes and get temporary space or NATs; install and test changes that make the network renumbering-friendly; plan the actual renumbering (phased or total, with a plan of retreat if major problems develop); take final backups; cut over addresses and names or begin coexistence, making DNS and firewall changes, restarting and clearing caches, and coordinating with ISPs, partners and routing registries; and document what is not yet documented. The guide also says plainly to take backups first of router configurations and DNS zone files.

To avoid instability, change one part of a routing hierarchy at a time, for example renumber a stub and let it stabilize, or add new numbers to the backbone, renumber the stubs, then remove the old backbone numbers. If a block of addresses must simply be reassigned, some loss of service must be expected.

The security section is short: configuration errors during renumbering can expose systems or deny service to authorized users, so filters must be right for both old and new addresses, and it may be appropriate to introduce authentication of routing updates.
sections.eli5: Moving day goes best with a checklist: list everything, pack a backup box, move one room at a time, and keep a plan for if things go wrong.
